title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter LI
paragraphs: Ladislaw had still heard no gossip about Mr. Casaubon's will. The dissolution of Parliament and the coming election filled the air, like the competing din of travelling shows at the old fairs and festivals; more private disturbances attracted little attention. The famous “dry election” was approaching, when the depth of public feeling could be measured by how low the tide of drink had fallen. Will Ladislaw was among the busiest people just then. Although Dorothea's widowhood was constantly on his mind, he had no desire to discuss it. When Lydgate sought him out to report their conversation about the Lowick living, he answered rather sharply—

“Why bring me into it? I never see Mrs. Casaubon, and I'm unlikely to while she's at Freshitt. I don't go there. It's Tory territory: the ‘Pioneer’ and I are about as welcome as a poacher with his gun.”

In fact, Will had become especially sensitive after noticing a change in Mr. Brooke. Previously Brooke had wanted him at the Grange more often than Will himself cared to go; now he seemed to arrange matters so that Will went there as little as possible. This was Mr. Brooke's evasive concession to Sir James Chettam's indignant protests. Will, alert to the faintest suggestion of this sort, concluded that he was being kept from the Grange because of Dorothea. So her friends were suspicious of him? Their fears were wholly unnecessary. If they imagined he would present himself as a penniless adventurer courting a wealthy woman's favour, they were badly mistaken.

Will had never fully understood the gulf between himself and Dorothea until now, when he stood at its edge and saw her on the opposite side. With some inward fury he began considering leaving the neighbourhood. He could show no further interest in her without exposing himself to unpleasant accusations—perhaps even in her own mind, which others might try to poison.

“We're separated for ever,” Will told himself. “I might as well be in Rome; she couldn't be any further away.” But what we call despair is often merely the painful impatience of hope denied its nourishment. There were plenty of reasons to stay—public reasons for remaining at his post in a crisis, instead of abandoning Mr. Brooke just when he needed coaching for the election and so much direct and indirect canvassing remained to be done. Will disliked deserting his own chessmen in the middle of a game. Any candidate on the right side might help secure a majority, even if his brains and backbone were as soft as a gentleman's bearing would allow. Coaching Mr. Brooke was difficult: he had to be kept steadily committed to voting for the actual Reform Bill, instead of insisting on his independence and his ability to pull back in time. Mr. Farebrother's prediction of a fourth candidate “in the bag” had not yet come true. Neither the Parliamentary Candidate Society nor any other body watching for ways to secure a reforming majority saw a difficulty worth intervening in while a second reform candidate, Mr. Brooke, might win a seat at his own expense. The contest remained entirely between Pinkerton, the old Tory member; Bagster, the new Whig member elected last time; and Brooke, the future independent member, who would bind himself to a party only on this occasion. Mr. Hawley and his allies would devote all their strength to electing Pinkerton. Brooke could succeed only through voters casting their sole vote for him and leaving Bagster behind, or through turning Tory votes into Reform votes. Naturally, the second method was preferable.

The hope of converting voters dangerously distracted Mr. Brooke. He believed wavering voters might be attracted by wavering statements; moreover, whenever opposing arguments resurfaced in his memory, his mind tended to catch on them again. Both habits caused Will Ladislaw considerable trouble.

“There are tactics in these matters, you know,” Mr. Brooke said. “Meeting people halfway—moderating your views—saying, ‘Well now, there's something in that,’ and so forth. I agree this is a special occasion—the country expressing its own will—political unions—that sort of thing. But sometimes we use rather too sharp a knife, Ladislaw. Take these ten-pound householders: why ten? Draw a line somewhere, yes—but why exactly ten? Once you examine it, that's a difficult question.”

“Of course it is,” Will said impatiently. “But if you're going to wait for a logically perfect Bill, you'll have to stand as a revolutionary, and I doubt Middlemarch would elect you then. This is no time to sit on the fence.”

Mr. Brooke always ended by agreeing with Ladislaw, whom he still regarded as a kind of Burke with a dash of Shelley. Before long, however, the wisdom of his own methods reasserted itself, and he returned to them full of hope. At this stage he was in excellent spirits, even when required to advance large sums of money. His powers of persuasion had not yet faced anything harder than a chairman's speech introducing other speakers, or a conversation with a Middlemarch voter. He came away from these encounters feeling he was a born tactician, and regretting that he had not entered this field sooner. With Mr. Mawmsey, though, he felt some sense of defeat. Mawmsey was a leading Middlemarch representative of that great social force, the retail trader, and naturally one of the borough's most uncertain voters. Personally he was happy to supply equally good tea and sugar to reformers and their opponents, and to agree impartially with both. Like the burgesses of earlier days, he felt that having to elect members of Parliament was a heavy burden on a town. Even if it were safe to encourage every party's hopes beforehand, in the end he would have to disappoint respectable customers whose names appeared in his accounts. Mr. Brooke of Tipton regularly placed large orders with him. On the other hand, many members of Pinkerton's committee had opinions backed by substantial grocery purchases. Judging that Mr. Brooke was not too “clever in his intellects,” Mawmsey thought him more likely to forgive a grocer pressured into voting against him. In his back parlour, he therefore spoke confidentially.

“Look at Reform from a family point of view, sir,” he said, pleasantly smiling and jingling the small silver coins in his pocket. “Will it support Mrs. Mawmsey and help her raise six children when I'm gone? I ask the question _fictiously_, knowing what the answer must be. Very well, sir. Tell me what a husband and father is to do when gentlemen come in and say, ‘Please yourself, Mawmsey, but if you vote against us, I'll buy my groceries elsewhere. When I sweeten my drink, I like to know I'm serving my country by supporting tradesmen of the right political colour.’ Those exact words have been spoken to me, sir, from the very chair you're sitting in. Not by your honourable self, Mr. Brooke, of course.”

“No, no, no—that's narrow-minded, you know. Until my butler complains about your goods, Mr. Mawmsey,” Mr. Brooke reassured him, “until I hear you're sending bad sugar, spices—that sort of thing—I shall never tell him to shop elsewhere.”
“Sir, your humble servant, and much obliged,” said Mr. Mawmsey, feeling that politics had become a little clearer. “It would be a pleasure to vote for a gentleman who speaks so honourably.”

“Well, Mr. Mawmsey, you'd find it was the right thing to join our side. Reform will affect everyone eventually—a thoroughly popular measure. A sort of alphabet, you know, which must come first before you can move on. I quite agree that you must think of the family. But there's public spirit to consider. We're all one family, you know—we all share one cupboard. A vote, for instance: it might help men make their fortunes at the Cape. There's no telling what a vote may achieve.” Mr. Brooke ended with a sense of drifting a little out to sea, though he still enjoyed the voyage. Mr. Mawmsey's reply brought him sharply to a halt.

“Excuse me, sir, but I can't afford that. When I vote, I must know what I'm doing. With respect, I must consider the effect on my till and my ledger. Prices, I'll admit, are something nobody can fully account for. The sudden drops after you've bought a supply of currants—and currants won't keep—I've never understood the rights and wrongs of that myself. A rebuke to human pride, it is. But as for one family, I hope we'll still have debtors and creditors. They're not going to reform that out of existence, or I'd vote to keep things as they are. Personally, few men have less cause to demand change than I do—for myself and my family, that is. I'm not a man with nothing to lose. I mean my standing in the parish and my private business, and nothing concerning your honourable self or your custom. You were kind enough to say you wouldn't withdraw that, whichever way I voted, so long as the goods supplied were satisfactory.”
Afterwards Mr. Mawmsey went upstairs and boasted to his wife that he had rather outwitted Brooke of Tipton. Going to the poll no longer troubled him quite so much.

On this occasion Mr. Brooke did not boast of his tactics to Ladislaw. Will, for his part, was happy to believe he had no involvement in canvassing except through reasoned argument, and used no less honourable instrument than knowledge. Naturally, Mr. Brooke had agents who understood the Middlemarch voter and knew how to recruit his ignorance in favour of the Bill. Their methods were remarkably similar to those for recruiting it against the Bill. Will closed his ears. Sometimes Parliament could scarcely carry on if we imagined its processes too vividly; the same is true of the rest of our lives, even our food and clothes. There were enough dirty-handed men in the world to handle dirty business. Will assured himself that his own part in getting Mr. Brooke elected would be entirely innocent.

Still, he seriously doubted whether this way of helping secure a majority for the right side would succeed. He had written several speeches and sets of speaking notes. But he was beginning to see that if Mr. Brooke's mind had to carry a train of thought, it would drop it, run off looking for it, and struggle to return. Collecting documents is one way of serving your country; remembering what they contain is another. No—the only way to force Mr. Brooke to think of the right arguments at the right moment was to feed him so many of them that nothing else would fit in his brain. Finding space was the difficulty: so much had already been stored there. Mr. Brooke himself remarked that his ideas tended to get in the way when he spoke.

Ladislaw's coaching would shortly be tested. Before nomination day Mr. Brooke was to explain his position to Middlemarch's worthy electors from the White Hart's balcony. It occupied a useful angle of the marketplace, overlooking a broad space and two streets converging upon it. The May morning was fine, and the outlook promising. An agreement between Bagster's committee and Brooke's seemed possible. Mr. Bulstrode, Mr. Standish in his capacity as a Liberal lawyer, and manufacturers including Mr. Plymdale and Mr. Vincy gave Brooke's committee a weight nearly equal to that of Mr. Hawley and his associates, who met for Pinkerton at the Green Dragon. Mr. Brooke knew that six months of improving his conduct as a landlord had blunted the “Trumpet's” attacks. Hearing a few cheers as he drove into town, he felt fairly light-hearted beneath his buff waistcoat. Yet at critical occasions, every moment often seems comfortably far away until the last one arrives.
“This looks promising, eh?” said Mr. Brooke as people gathered. “I'll have a good audience, at least. I enjoy this—a crowd made up of one's own neighbours, you know.”

Unlike Mr. Mawmsey, Middlemarch's weavers and tanners had never considered Mr. Brooke a neighbour. They felt no more attachment to him than if he had arrived in a box from London. Nevertheless, they listened fairly quietly to the speakers introducing him. One, a political figure from Brassing who had come to explain Middlemarch's duty, spoke at such length that it was alarming to wonder what he could leave the candidate to say. Meanwhile the crowd thickened. As the political personage approached his conclusion, Mr. Brooke experienced a remarkable change in his feelings. Outwardly he continued handling his eyeglass, fiddling with the papers before him and chatting to his committee, as though wholly indifferent to when he was called upon.

“I'll have another sherry, Ladislaw,” he said casually to Will, standing close behind him. Will soon supplied the supposed restorative. It was a poor choice. Mr. Brooke drank little, and quickly taking a second glass so soon after the first startled his system, scattering his energies instead of concentrating them. Do feel sorry for him. So many English gentlemen make themselves miserable giving speeches for wholly private purposes! Mr. Brooke wished to serve his country by standing for Parliament—something that may also be done for private purposes, certainly, but once undertaken it absolutely requires speeches.

The opening did not worry him. He was certain of that; he would have it ready, neatly cut and finished as a few couplets from Pope. Getting aboard would be easy. The prospect of the open sea afterwards was frightening. “And questions,” suggested the demon beginning to stir in his stomach, “someone might ask questions about the schedules.—Ladislaw,” he went on aloud, “pass me the notes on the schedules, will you?”

When Mr. Brooke stepped onto the balcony, the cheers easily balanced the yells, groans, brays and other expressions of opposing views. Indeed, these were so restrained that Mr. Standish, an old campaigner, remarked into the nearest ear, “By God, this looks dangerous! Hawley's planned something deeper than this.” Still, the cheering was encouraging. No candidate could have looked more amiable than Mr. Brooke, his notes in his breast pocket, his left hand resting on the railing and his right playing with his eyeglass. His most noticeable features were the buff waistcoat, closely clipped fair hair and uncommitted expression. He began confidently enough.
“Gentlemen—electors of Middlemarch!”
This was exactly the proper beginning, and a brief pause after it seemed quite natural.
“I'm extraordinarily pleased to be here. I've never felt so proud and happy in my life—never so happy, you know.”

That was a bold figure of speech, though not quite the right one. Unfortunately his polished opening had vanished. Even Pope's couplets may become “fallings from us, vanishings” when fear grips us and a glass of sherry rushes like smoke through our thoughts. Standing at the window behind him, Ladislaw thought, “That's finished it. Our only hope is that since the best thing doesn't always work, floundering might work for once.” Mr. Brooke, deprived of other guides, fell back on himself and his qualifications—always a suitable, graceful subject for a candidate.

“My good friends, I'm your near neighbour. You've known me as a magistrate for years. I've always examined public questions closely—machinery, for example, and machine-breaking. Many of you work with machinery, and I've been studying that lately. Breaking machines won't do, you know. Everything must continue—trade, manufacturing, commerce, exchanging staple goods—all that. Since Adam Smith, it has to continue. We must survey the whole globe: ‘Observation with extensive view’ must look everywhere, ‘from China to Peru,’ as someone says. Johnson, I think—‘The Rambler,’ you know. I've done that myself, to a point—not as far as Peru. But I haven't always stayed at home; I saw that wouldn't do. I've visited the Levant, where some of your Middlemarch goods are sold—and the Baltic too. Now, the Baltic.”

Sailing among his memories like this, Mr. Brooke might have proceeded comfortably enough and returned from the furthest seas without difficulty. But the enemy had arranged a devilish intervention. At the very same moment, almost directly opposite him and less than ten yards away, an effigy of himself rose above the crowd's shoulders. Buff waistcoat, eyeglass and neutral face were painted on cloth. With it came an echo of his words, parrot-like and shrill as Punch, apparently floating in the air like a cuckoo's call. Everyone looked up at the open windows where the two streets met, but they were either empty or occupied by laughing spectators. Even the most innocent echo sounds impishly mocking when it follows a solemn, persistent speaker. This echo was far from innocent. It lacked a natural echo's precision, but maliciously selected the words it caught. By the time it repeated “Now, the Baltic,” the laughter rippling through the crowd became a general roar. Only party loyalties and the great public cause which tangled circumstances had attached to “Brooke of Tipton” kept his own committee from joining in. Mr. Bulstrode sternly demanded to know what the new police were doing. But one could hardly arrest a voice, and attacking the effigy would send an ambiguous message, since Hawley probably intended it to be pelted.

Mr. Brooke himself was scarcely capable of noticing anything except the general flight of ideas from his own mind. His ears even rang a little. He alone had not yet properly registered either the echo or his own image. Few things imprison our perceptions more completely than anxiety over what to say next. He heard the laughter, but had expected Tory attempts at disruption. Besides, he was now excited by the tingling sense that his lost introduction was returning to bring him home from the Baltic.

“That reminds me,” he continued, slipping one hand casually into a side pocket, “if I needed a precedent, you know—though we never need a precedent for doing right—there's Chatham, for instance. I can't say I would have supported Chatham, or Pitt—the younger Pitt. He wasn't a man of ideas, and ideas are what we need, you know.”
“Damn your ideas! We want the Bill!” shouted a rough voice from below.

The unseen Punch, which until then had followed Mr. Brooke, instantly repeated, “Damn your ideas! We want the Bill!” Laughter burst out louder than ever. For the first time, being silent himself, Mr. Brooke distinctly heard the mocking echo. But it seemed to be mocking the man who had interrupted him, which was encouraging. He therefore replied pleasantly—

“There's something in what you say, my good friend. Why else do we gather, except to speak our minds—freedom of opinion, freedom of the press, liberty—all that? Now, the Bill—you shall have the Bill.” He paused to fit his eyeglass and draw the paper from his breast pocket, feeling that he was becoming practical and specific. The invisible Punch took up the words—
“You shall have the bill, Mr. Brooke: for one election contest, with a seat outside Parliament, as delivered—five thousand pounds, seven shillings and fourpence.”

Amid the roaring laughter, Mr. Brooke flushed and dropped his eyeglass. Looking round in confusion, he caught sight of his effigy, now closer than before. A moment later he saw it woefully splattered with eggs. His courage rose a little, and so did his voice.

“Clowning, tricks, ridicule as the test of truth—all very well—” At this point a disagreeable egg broke on Mr. Brooke's shoulder, while the echo repeated, “All very well.” A shower of eggs followed, mostly aimed at the effigy, but occasionally striking the original as though by accident. Fresh men streamed into the crowd. Whistles, screams, bellows and fifes swelled the uproar, made louder still by the shouting and struggling of those trying to suppress it. No voice could have carried above such a din. Unpleasantly anointed, Mr. Brooke abandoned his position. The defeat would have been less maddening had it been less playful and schoolboyish. A serious assault, which a reporter “can aver that it endangered the learned gentleman's ribs,” or respectfully describe as leaving “the soles of that gentleman's boots having been visible above the railing,” might offer more consolation.

Mr. Brooke returned to the committee room, saying as lightly as he could, “That's rather too bad, you know. I'd have won their attention eventually, but they gave me no time. I'd have explained the Bill in due course, you know,” he added with a glance at Ladislaw. “Still, it'll all come right at the nomination.”
There was no unanimous confidence that it would. On the contrary, the committee looked grim, while the political visitor from Brassing wrote busily, apparently devising fresh plans.

“Bowyer was behind it,” Mr. Standish said evasively. “I'm as certain as if he'd advertised himself. He's exceptionally good at ventriloquism, and by God, he did that exceptionally well! Hawley's been inviting him to dinner lately. Bowyer has a fund of talent.”
“Well, Standish, you never mentioned him. Otherwise I'd have invited him myself,” said poor Mr. Brooke, who had done a great deal of inviting for his country's sake.
“There's no more contemptible fellow in Middlemarch than Bowyer,” Ladislaw said angrily. “Yet it always seems to be the contemptible fellows who tip the balance.”

Will was thoroughly angry with himself as well as with his employer. He shut himself in his rooms, half resolved to abandon both Mr. Brooke and the “Pioneer.” Why stay? If the impassable gulf between himself and Dorothea could ever be bridged, it would be by leaving and winning a completely different position, not by remaining here and sinking into deserved contempt as Brooke's subordinate. Then came the youthful dream of the wonders he might achieve—in five years, say. Political writing and speaking would count for more now that public life was becoming broader and more national. They might win him enough distinction that he would no longer seem to be asking Dorothea to step down to his level. Five years—if only he knew she cared for him more than for other men; if only he could make her understand that he kept his distance until he could declare his love without degrading himself. Then he could leave readily and embark on a career that seemed perfectly plausible at twenty-five, according to the mind's inward arrangement of things, where talent brings fame and fame brings every other delight. He could speak and write; he could master any subject he chose. He always intended to stand for reason and justice, bringing all his passion to their side. Why should he not one day rise above the crowd and feel he had earned his eminence? Certainly he would leave Middlemarch, go to London and prepare himself for distinction by “eating his dinners” as a student of law.

But not immediately—not until he and Dorothea had exchanged some kind of sign. He would not be satisfied until she understood why, even if he were the man she chose, he would refuse to marry her. So he must remain at his post and tolerate Mr. Brooke a little longer.

Before long, however, he had reason to suspect that Mr. Brooke had anticipated his wish to end their association. Outside delegations and voices closer to home had together persuaded that philanthropist to take an unusually decisive step for humanity's benefit: he would withdraw in favour of another candidate, leaving that man the advantages of his canvassing organization. Mr. Brooke called this a strong measure, but remarked that his health could bear less excitement than he had supposed.

“I've had some discomfort in my chest. One mustn't push that too far,” he explained to Ladislaw. “I must pull back. Poor Casaubon was a warning, you know. I've advanced some substantial sums, but I've dug a channel. It's rather rough work, this electioneering, eh, Ladislaw? I dare say you're tired of it. Still, we've dug a channel with the ‘Pioneer’—set things going, and so forth. A more ordinary man than you could keep it going now—someone more ordinary, you know.”
“Do you want me to give it up?” Will asked, colour rushing into his face. He rose from the writing table and paced three steps with his hands in his pockets. “I'm ready to do so whenever you wish.”

“As for wishing, my dear Ladislaw, you know how highly I rate your abilities. But I've been discussing the ‘Pioneer’ with some men on our side. They're inclined to take it over—reimburse me to some extent—and run it themselves. Under the circumstances, you might prefer to leave—find a better field for your talents. These people might not appreciate you as I always have, as an alter ego, a right hand. Though I've always expected you to go on to something else. I'm thinking of a little trip to France. But I'll write whatever introductions you need, you know—to Althorpe and people like that. I've met Althorpe.”
“I'm extremely obliged to you,” Ladislaw replied proudly. “Since you're parting with the ‘Pioneer,’ I needn't trouble you with my own plans. I may decide to stay here for the present.”

Once Mr. Brooke had gone, Will told himself, “The rest of the family have been pressing him to get rid of me, and now he doesn't mind if I leave. I'll stay as long as I please. I'll go when I choose, not because they're afraid of me.”
